## Proof

We construct an infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ of positive integers, each of the form $2^n - 3$ ($n \ge 2$), such that every pair is relatively prime.

**Base case.** Set $a_1 = 2^3 - 3 = 5$. A single-element set is vacuously pairwise coprime.

**Inductive step.** Suppose $a_1, \dots, a_k$ are pairwise coprime, each of the form $a_i = 2^{n_i} - 3$ with $n_i \ge 2$. Note each $a_i$ is **odd** (since $2^{n_i}$ is even and subtracting $3$ keeps it odd) and $a_i > 1$.

Since $\gcd(2, a_i) = 1$, the multiplicative order $d_i = \operatorname{ord}_{a_i}(2)$ is well defined. Because $a_i > 2$, we have $2 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{a_i}$, so $d_i \ge 2$. Let

$$N = \operatorname{lcm}(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k).$$

Then $N \ge 2$, and $2^N \equiv 1 \pmod{a_i}$ for every $i$. Define

$$a_{k+1} = 2^N - 3.$$

This is a positive integer of the required form (since $N \ge 2$). We claim it is coprime to every $a_i$.

Indeed, $2^N \equiv 1 \pmod{a_i}$ gives

$$a_{k+1} = 2^N - 3 \equiv 1 - 3 = -2 \pmod{a_i}.$$

Hence any common divisor $d$ of $a_{k+1}$ and $a_i$ divides both $a_i$ and $-2$, so $d \mid \gcd(a_i, 2)$. But $a_i$ is odd, so $\gcd(a_i, 2) = 1$, forcing $d = 1$. Thus

$$\gcd(a_{k+1}, a_i) = 1 \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, k.$$

Since the $a_1, \dots, a_k$ were already pairwise coprime by the inductive hypothesis, the enlarged set $a_1, \dots, a_{k+1}$ is pairwise coprime.

**Termination / infinity.** Each step strictly increases the index and produces a new, larger integer ($N \ge 2$ and the orders grow, so $a_{k+1} > a_k$ in particular once $k \ge 1$). The construction therefore never cycles and yields infinitely many distinct terms.

By induction, for every $k$ we obtain $k$ pairwise coprime integers of the form $2^n - 3$; letting $k \to \infty$ gives an infinite set of positive integers of the form $2^n - 3$, every pair of which is relatively prime. $\blacksquare$
